title: Mejía weighs Mexico’s persistent food-service inflation against weaker demand
summary: Deputy Governor Omar Mejía Castelazo sees less risk that the latest energy shock will feed through to Mexican inflation than during the 2022 commodity shock. In his November presentation, he puts particular weight on the condition of the economy when prices began to rise. Demand has less momentum, global supply chains face less pressure and current monetary conditions still constrain spending in his assessment. He describes the monetary cycle that started in June 2021 as having ended in May 2026. The presentation gives his personal view of the stance and contains no new Governing Board decision or commitment on the date of its next move (cover and PDF pages 2–4).

The comparison with 2022 explains why an increase in crude oil can have different consequences for domestic prices. During the earlier episode the global supply-chain pressure indicator was around three standard deviations above its historical average. In the current episode it was around one. Annual growth in insured employment in the two comparison periods ranged from 4.4% to 5% and from zero to 1.4%, respectively. The slide also compares levels of inflation, domestic activity and the behaviour of US and Mexican petrol prices. These are differences in the conditions under which a shock propagates. They give no precise estimate of how much an additional dollar on a barrel of oil would add to Mexican consumer prices (PDF pages 3–4).

Several price movements require separate explanations. On PDF pages 5–7, changes in fruit and vegetable prices affect annual non-core inflation in part because of the prices recorded a year earlier. Goods prices identified as particularly sensitive to imports show a downward trend, which Mejía reads as evidence of limited transmission from supply-chain disruption. Services inflation has eased more gradually. Meals eaten away from home remain an important source of persistence, and services inflation still exceeds pre-pandemic norms. The cost breakdown on PDF page 10 matters here. Food services use less labour relative to other inputs than some other services do. Their prices can therefore respond to changes in ingredients as well as wages. The presentation does not estimate the separate contribution from each input.

On the demand side, the growth fan chart points to moderate expansion, against a backdrop of uneven consumption, investment and manufacturing exports. There is scope for closer trade integration, particularly in equipment related to technology investment. That opportunity can coexist with spare capacity in the domestic economy. Mejía sets the estimated output gap alongside a broader slack indicator drawn from eleven series. His comparison of the forward-looking real policy rate with an estimated neutral range uses the overnight rate target and survey expectations for inflation over the next twelve months. Both the neutral rate and potential output are estimates, and the historical comparisons depend on which inflation observations enter the sample (PDF pages 11–17 and 21).

Mejía also asks how restraint reaches households and firms. PDF pages 18–20 compare term-deposit rates with the policy rate, separate liquid household saving from term instruments and distinguish rates on new bank loans from growth in outstanding credit. An estimated credit response to a 25-basis-point policy shock varies with the strength of activity and develops over several quarters. The presentation describes long-term expectations as anchored, drawing on survey means and the distribution of five-to-eight-year forecasts. For someone judging the persistence of Mexican inflation, the observations to reconcile are the prices still rising in services, the composition of domestic slack and whether long-horizon expectations remain stable as near-term prices change.

questions.question: Would another increase in energy prices begin to move five-to-eight-year inflation expectations?
questions.detail: Mejía’s assessment depends partly on the stability of longer-horizon survey responses. A movement in the upper part of their distribution could precede a visible change in the mean. Compare successive vintages of the same private-sector survey with petrol and imported-goods prices, and separate revisions to near-term forecasts from changes reported by the same forecasters at the longer horizon.

questions.question: How much of the persistence in meals away from home reflects food inputs rather than labour costs?
questions.detail: The cost chart establishes that restaurants and similar businesses use a different input mix from other service providers. It does not estimate how quickly each cost is passed on. Track producer or wholesale food prices, wages and consumer prices for the restaurant categories shown, allowing for different lags. The answer would affect how much weight food-service inflation deserves as a signal of domestic demand.

questions.question: How sensitive is the assessment of restraint to the chosen neutral rate and measure of slack?
questions.detail: A twelve-month inflation expectation, an estimated neutral range and an estimate of productive capacity all enter the comparisons. Recalculate the real-rate gap with alternative survey expectations and examine the constituent activity indicators as they are revised. Compare those results with the rates actually available on new loans and deposits. This would show whether different plausible measures imply a similar degree of restraint.
